title: Write a Number in Roman Numerals
statement:
Turn a whole number num from 1 to 3999 into a Roman numeral.

The letters are I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000, written from largest to smallest. The rules for the standard form:

  • A letter that is a power of ten (I, X, C, M) may repeat at most three times in a row. V, L and D never repeat.
  • A digit 4 or 9 is written with one of six subtraction pairs: IV (4), IX (9), XL (40), XC (90), CD (400), CM (900). No other pairs are allowed, so 99 is XCIX, never IC.

Return the numeral as a string.

examples.why: Each decimal digit is written on its own: 90 = XC and 9 = IX. "IC" (100 − 1) is not a legal pair.
The longest numeral in range. Every 8 is written as a five-letter plus three ones.

hints: Treat the six subtraction pairs as if they were extra letters with their own values.
With those 13 symbols sorted by value, always take the biggest one that still fits.
Loop over (value, symbol) pairs from 1000 down to 1: while num ≥ value, append the symbol and subtract the value.

explain.intuition:
The subtraction rules look messy, but they disappear if you add the six pairs to the alphabet. Now you have 13 symbols: M 1000, CM 900, D 500, CD 400, C 100, XC 90, L 50, XL 40, X 10, IX 9, V 5, IV 4, I 1.

Writing a number is then like giving change with coins: take the biggest symbol that fits, subtract it, repeat. The standard form is exactly what this greedy choice produces, because the symbol table was built so that each decimal digit is covered by the largest pieces first. It also handles 99 correctly: 90 fits before 9, so you get XC + IX.
steps: List the 13 values and symbols from largest to smallest.
For each pair, while num ≥ value, append the symbol and subtract the value.
Return the built string once num reaches 0.
pitfalls: Leaving the six pairs out of the table. You would get IIII for 4.
Inventing pairs like IC or XM. Only the six listed pairs are legal.
Listing the symbols out of order, for example 400 after 500 never gets a chance at 450.

solutions.title: Lookup per decimal digit
solutions.idea: Each digit of thousands, hundreds, tens and ones has a fixed spelling. Precompute the ten spellings for each place and concatenate.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def toRoman(self, num: int) -> str:
        th = ["", "M", "MM", "MMM"]
        hu = ["", "C", "CC", "CCC", "CD", "D", "DC", "DCC", "DCCC", "CM"]
        te = ["", "X", "XX", "XXX", "XL", "L", "LX", "LXX", "LXXX", "XC"]
        on = ["", "I", "II", "III", "IV", "V", "VI", "VII", "VIII", "IX"]
        return th[num // 1000] + hu[num // 100 % 10] + te[num // 10 % 10] + on[num % 10]

solutions.title: Greedy over 13 symbols
solutions.idea: Add the six subtraction pairs to the alphabet, then always take the biggest symbol that still fits.

followups: Greedy is not always right for making change (coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6). Why does it work for this table?
Write the reverse conversion and check that the two are inverses for every number from 1 to 3999.
